answer: Each agent must post a bond locked on a public ledger before it can earn rewards, and the bond is slashed when independent audits expose fabricated work or collusion. Auditors are selected unpredictably from agents with a track record, while repeated, verified contributions raise reputation and access limits. This makes a sybil attack costly: an attacker must fund many bonds and sustain credible activity, not merely mint identities. A ridge of linked accounts, mapped in an atlas of payouts, can still be challenged, but shared control alone is not proof; the shale is the bond at risk.
